questions.stem: When aqueous copper sulfate is electrolysed with inert electrodes, copper is deposited at the cathode rather than hydrogen. Why is copper produced instead of hydrogen?

options.text: Copper ions are smaller than hydrogen ions
Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so copper ions are preferentially discharged
There are no hydrogen ions present in the solution
Hydrogen can only be produced from acids

questions.explanation: In aqueous solutions, both the metal ion and H+ ions from water compete for discharge at the cathode. The less reactive ion is preferentially discharged. Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so Cu2+ ions are discharged in preference to H+ ions. Water does provide H+ ions, but they remain in solution.

questions.stem: A student electrolyses dilute sodium chloride solution with inert electrodes. What products would form at the cathode and anode?

options.text: Sodium at the cathode; chlorine at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode; chlorine at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode; oxygen at the anode
Sodium at the cathode; oxygen at the anode

questions.explanation: Sodium is very reactive (above hydrogen), so H+ ions from water are discharged at the cathode instead, producing hydrogen gas. At the anode, with a dilute solution, there are not enough Cl- ions, so OH- ions from water are discharged instead, producing oxygen. With concentrated NaCl, chlorine would be produced at the anode.

questions.stem: During electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution (brine), the solution gradually becomes alkaline. Which ion is responsible for this and why?

options.text: Na+ ions accumulate because sodium is not discharged
OH- ions accumulate because H+ ions are discharged at the cathode, leaving excess OH-
Cl- ions make the solution alkaline
The chlorine gas dissolves to make the solution alkaline

questions.explanation: Water dissociates into H+ and OH- ions. At the cathode, H+ ions are preferentially discharged (2H+ + 2e- -> H2), removing them from solution. The OH- ions remain in solution and are not removed, making the solution increasingly alkaline. Na+ ions also remain, forming NaOH solution.

questions.stem: When concentrated hydrochloric acid is electrolysed, hydrogen is produced at the cathode and chlorine at the anode. What are the half-equations for these reactions?

options.text: Cathode: 2H+ + 2e- -> H2; Anode: 2Cl- - 2e- -> Cl2
Cathode: H2 -> 2H+ + 2e-; Anode: Cl2 -> 2Cl- + 2e-
Cathode: 2H+ -> H2 + 2e-; Anode: 2Cl- + 2e- -> Cl2
Cathode: H+ + e- -> H; Anode: Cl- -> Cl + e-

questions.explanation: At the cathode, H+ ions gain electrons (reduction): 2H+ + 2e- -> H2. At the anode, Cl- ions lose electrons (oxidation): 2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e- (also written as 2Cl- - 2e- -> Cl2). Option B shows the reverse reactions. Option D does not show the formation of diatomic molecules.

questions.stem: A student electrolyses aqueous copper sulfate with inert (carbon) electrodes and notices the blue colour of the solution fading over time. Why does this happen?

options.text: The sulfate ions are being used up at the anode
The water is evaporating, diluting the solution
Cu2+ ions are being removed from solution as they are deposited as copper at the cathode
The carbon electrodes are absorbing the blue colour

questions.explanation: The blue colour of copper sulfate solution is due to Cu2+ ions. During electrolysis, Cu2+ ions migrate to the cathode and are reduced to copper metal (Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu), which deposits on the electrode. As Cu2+ ions are removed from solution, the concentration decreases and the blue colour fades.
